cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Declare Allegiance
cards.instruction: Make someone choose which person, side, or claim to authority they will support.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I've approved your help at the chess club election. Will you wear my ribbon or Nina's?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You may remain friends with both of us. I'm asking which of us you want as chair.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Could I wear yours today and hers tomorrow?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Tomorrow's the vote. I won't approve a timetable that postpones your answer until voting day. Tell me now whose ribbon you'll wear to vote.

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 presumes authority over B help; A3 grants friendship and A5 denies a postponing timetable, using approval to force vote-day allegiance.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 friendship concern produces A3 permission and chair distinction; B4 day rotation produces A5 deadline clarification without invented ribbon ownership.

relationship.evidence: B2 values both friendships and B4 offers a workable social compromise that A rejects for its evasive electoral meaning.

heightening.evidence: B4 tomorrow rotation causes A5 to insist now on the consequential vote-day sign, tightening the choice rather than adding a random test.

specificity.evidence: A1 election and B4 two-day schedule are legible; A5 establishes tomorrow as voting day with no unsupported absence of A.

brevityWit.evidence: A3 permission to remain friends is dry status wit; A5 explanation is clear but less economical than the strongest examples.
